sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Cybersecurity—and especially the niche of Digital Forensics—has long been associated with notoriously unapproachable user interfaces, difficult user experiences, and confusing application flows. From bloated, messy logs to outdated design trends, there are plenty of reasons for this reputation. As we discussed problems we were passionate about solving, a common thread emerged from our diverse professional and technical backgrounds. Many mission-critical tools in Digital Forensics are nearly impossible for amateur or untrained users to navigate, too intimidating to encourage broader adoption, and simply unenjoyable to use. By combining our team’s strengths in graphical design, user experience, and cybersecurity engineering, we created Forens.tech—an application designed to change that narrative.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Forens.tech takes an innovative approach to common digital forensics techniques—combining a fresh, well-planned, and deliberate user experience with reliable methods to quickly parse and display memory dump data. Forens.tech is a web application that runs locally on a customer’s system, alongside any memory dump files they wish to analyze. It offers a straightforward, easy-to-follow selection process for choosing the types of scans to run on the selected file, using those inputs to execute Volatility3 for analysis. The application outputs a consistently clean and structured JSON result, which is then passed to a Gemini-powered LLM agent for summarization and deeper insight. This includes both objective data and a cleaned-up version of the command output, all presented clearly to the end user. Using Volatility3, Forens.tech can offer options for analysis on a system’s running processes, conducting a file scan of the computer, getting OS information, viewing network connections, and returning a list of executed system commands. The goal is to simplify memory dump analysis, making it more accessible to a wider audience of law enforcement and blue team specialists. Along with this focus, utilizing tools like Volatility3, Forens.tech can offer a wide range of expanding options to analyze data from the position of beginners to experienced professionals.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Forens.tech’s front end was built using ReactJS and custom CSS after analyzing multiple design features with prototypes using Figma. As a team, we had to think about who the intended end-use_r was and their unique descriptors, such as location, age, mental states, and hobbies. To be on the same page of things, we collectively created the _task flow in FigJam. Following that, we created the wireframe , this helped us figure out what was capable on both sides of the front-end development and back-end development. Then, we took into account typography, contrast checking, coloring, and style guides to then land on the high fidelity prototypes. We made sure that these prototypes were user-friendly and accessible to the intended user personas. For back-end, Volatility3 is called through a Python script, which pushes output through fastapi to serve mission-critical information to the end user.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One major challenge was using Volatility and learning to work with memory dumps, both of which are things none of our team members had prior experience with. Luckily, both the documentation and usage are relatively straightforward and well-maintained, allowing for the creation of our automated scripts to come after a few hours of initial research.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Our team is incredibly proud of how well the interface came out for Forens.tech. Although it was difficult at times, ensuring to build with a focus on the user interface and being deliberate with our design decisions helped us to create a good-looking and good-performing web application..

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: In addition to deepening our understanding of memory dumps and how tools like Volatility3 support cyber professionals in incident response, we also gained valuable insight into the importance of planning and preparation—and the significant impact they have on the quality of an application’s visual design, cognitive psychology, and user interface.

sections.heading: What's next for Forens.tech

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We often found ourselves stuck at the start of the design process, not knowing where to begin or how to turn our ideas into something real. In large organisations these issues are not only inconvenient and costly, but also slow down development. That is why we created ConArt AI to make it easier. It helps teams get their ideas out quickly and turn them into something real without all the confusion.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: ConArt AI is a gamified design application that helps artists and teams brainstorm ideas faster in the early stages of a project. Teams come together in a shared space where each person has to create a quick sketch and provide a prompt before the timer runs out. The sketches are then turned into images and everyone votes on their team's design where points are given from 1 to 5. This process encourages fast and fun brainstorming while helping teams quickly move from ideas to concepts. It makes collaboration more engaging and helps speed up the creative process.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built ConArt AI using React for the frontend to create a smooth and responsive interface that allows for real-time collaboration. On the backend, we used Convex to handle game logic and state management, ensuring seamless communication between players during the sketching, voting, and scoring phases. For the image generation, we integrated the Replicate API, which utilises AI models like ControlNet with Stable Diffusion to transform the sketches and prompts into full-fledged concept images. These API calls are managed through Convex actions, allowing for real-time updates and feedback loops. The entire project is hosted on Vercel, which is officially supported by Convex, ensuring fast deployment and scaling. Convex especially enabled us to have a serverless experience which allowed us to not worry about extra infrastructure and focus more on the functions of our app. The combination of these technologies allows ConArt AI to deliver a gamified, collaborative experience.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We faced several challenges while building ConArt AI. One of the key issues was with routing in production, where we had to troubleshoot differences between development and live environments. We also encountered challenges in managing server vs. client-side actions, particularly ensuring smooth, real-time updates. Additionally, we had some difficulties with responsive design, ensuring the app looked and worked well across different devices and screen sizes. These challenges pushed us to refine our approach and improve the overall performance of the application.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re incredibly proud of several key accomplishments from this hackathon. Nikhil: Learned how to use a new service like Convex during the hackathon, adapting quickly to integrate it into our project. Ben: Instead of just showcasing a local demo, he managed to finish and fully deploy the project by the end of the hackathon, which is a huge achievement. Shireen: Completed the UI/UX design of a website in under 36 hours for the first time, while also planning our pitch and brand identity, all during her first hackathon. Ryushen: He worked on building React components and the frontend, ensuring the UI/UX looked pretty, while also helping to craft an awesome pitch. Overall, we’re most proud of how well we worked as a team. Every person filled their role and brought the project to completion, and we’re happy to have made new friends along the way!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to effectively use Convex by studying its documentation, which helped us manage real-time state and game logic for features like live sketching, voting, and scoring. We also learned how to trigger external API calls, like image generation with Replicate, through Convex actions, making the integration of AI seamless. On top of that, we improved our collaboration as a team, dividing tasks efficiently and troubleshooting together, which was key to building ConArt AI successfully.

We will also be adding a feature to save concept art, allowing teams to store and revisit their designs for future reference or iteration. These updates will enhance collaboration and creativity, making ConArt AI even more valuable for artists and teams working on long-term projects.

devpost_page.tagline: The city sinks at the end of the year. Your money decides if you're on the last ship.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Finance is a very daunting subject. A lot of games have tried to make it fun, but none of them seemed to click for us. So, we decided to create our own finance game that's actually fun, not just looking through spreadsheets and technical analysis, and it still actually teaches you how to make good financial decisions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Atlantis is a 2D pixel-art game set in a sinking underwater city. The 'Council' has read the tides: Atlantis sinks after the Long Dark. One ship will leave, and Passage on it is sold for coin, only to people who owe nothing to anyone. You have one year to get on that ship: Four seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn and the Long Dark. Six tides each: every tide is one move. You work, trade at the Market, invest at the Harbor Exchange, borrow, save and pay down debt. A rising price: Passage costs 1,200◈ in Spring and climbs every season. Coin that just sits there falls behind. About ten minutes for a full run. Everyone starts somewhere different. Each of the four classes is built on a real financial barrier, and none is labelled by identity: The Newcomer: no credit history, so no card or loans until they build one with a secured card. First of Their Line: no family wealth, and starts 500◈ in debt to the guild. The Caretaker: care duties cost tides and coin every season, but they have a community lending circle. Every mechanic is a real money concept. Inside the game everything uses in-world names. Then the Modern Mirror , a gilded mirror button in every building, reveals the real thing behind it: Purse / Vault → Checking / savings account Leviathan Credit → Credit card (30% a year, minimum payments, late fees) Standing (300–850) → Credit score Harbor Exchange → Stock market The Tide Index → S&P 500 index fund Deepcoral Salvage → Penny stocks and lottery tickets The Council's debaseme

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Capital One Nessie is the money layer. Every coin movement in the game is a real banking record: Accounts: each class is its own Nessie customer with checking (Purse), savings (Vault) and a credit card account. Loans: the guild loan, the lending circle and Black Reef advances are loan records, kept current with PUT updates. Money movements: wages, sales and dividends are deposits. Market, Exchange and Passage spending are purchases at in-world merchants. Moving coin between Purse and Vault, and paying the card, are transfers. Confirmation: each money effect is queued, POSTed to Nessie, then read back with a GET to confirm it landed. Responses are cached locally, so the game keeps running if the API lags. The in-game Ledger: shows every Nessie record with its status and checks the Purse and Vault against Nessie's balances. A deterministic game engine (Python): Pure and seeded: its seeded so every run in different and unique. It makes the game much more fun to replay. One config file: every number in the game lives there. A balance simulator: bots play thousands of seeded years per class with different strategies (wages only, saver, gambler, kelp trader, diversified, thoughtful) so we can measure what numbers are actually fair to keep. The rest of the stack: Backend: FastAPI and Pydantic, with SQLite storing runs, actions and the Nessie queue. Frontend: React and TypeScript, plus Phaser 3 for the clickable underwater city: three rings of land and water, caustic light, swaying k

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making it fun and honest at once. Balancing took a lot of simulator runs. Early on, a few hundred coins invested earned less than the shift it cost to trade, so investing lost to saving. We made the first Market and Exchange visit each season free. We also found that money owed to the lending circle wasn't counted as debt, which let one class buy Passage in Spring, so we closed that loophole. Nessie in production. Some resources behaved differently from the docs. Bill reads returned errors, and transaction records didn't update account balances. We built a sync layer that confirms every record with a GET, holds later records behind unconfirmed ones, and only sends loan and bill records once they're verified live. Explaining a deep game quickly. Playtesters were lost at first. We added Chelo's guided tour, short plain explanations in every building, and the Modern Mirror. That way the real-world lesson arrives after you've felt the mechanic, not before.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A complete game: a full year, four classes, 14 market shocks, 13 Scrolls, a season report card, four endings, and a hand-built beautiful pixel-art city. Real banking behind every coin: each move is posted to Nessie and confirmed. Real barriers, not stereotypes: the classes change where you start, never the rules. Teaching by consequence: real-world finance terms appear only in the Modern Mirror. Everywhere else, you learn by playing.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: People remember what happened to them far longer than what they were told. A credit card that snowballed, or a fraud charge they forgot to dispute, sticks better than any definition. A deterministic, fully tested engine made balancing possible. We could change one number and see its effect across thousands of games in seconds. Building on a real banking API forces you to handle the messy parts: failures, retries, confirmations and records that don't behave as documented.

sections.heading: What's next for Atlantis - The Long Night
sections.text: A classroom mode with a shared seed, so a whole class plays the same year and compares choices. More starting classes based on other real barriers. Business ownership and bank loans. Both are already built in the engine and switched off until they're balanced. Sound, and a more dramatic Long Dark.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: College students meet new people all the time: at orientation, club fairs, hackathons, the person next to them in lecture. Almost none of those meetings turn into anything. You swap names, maybe follow each other, and never see them again. Social apps haven't helped. They're built to keep you scrolling, not to get you into a room with people. We wanted the opposite: a social app where the AI's job is getting you offline . We also noticed that the best new friends usually come through people you already know: a friend's roommate, someone your lab partner vouches for. So we built on that idea. You are a node, and every time you meet someone in person, an edge forms. Degreesº uses that real-world graph to put small groups of people together and send them out to do something. It's a dating app for friend groups.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Meet in person, and the graph grows. Scan someone's QR code, or join an event with a room code and tap "We met" next to the people you actually talked to. Each one becomes a first-degree connection. Hosts can run meetups, and ending one connects everyone who was there. You choose how far it reaches. Your "degrees" setting decides who you can be matched with: only people you've met, friends of friends, or the wider network. Group size, budget, travel distance and how often you want to meet are all yours to set. AI forms the group. Degreesº walks your connection graph, ranks candidates by how similar their interests are (Gemini embeddings), and has Gemini put together a small group with a plain-English explanation of why it fits. We deliberately include at least one friend-of-a-friend, because that's where new friendships come from. Privacy is enforced by the server, not just hidden in the UI. Anyone you haven't met stays anonymous until everyone in the group accepts. That applies to names, photos, bios, and even the AI's explanation. A real plan, not a suggestion. Gemini with Google Maps grounding picks a real venue that fits everyone's budget, interests and distance, and Places fills in the address, map pin and price. When Maps doesn't work out, it falls back to real ticketed events from Ticketmaster. Your group can ask for another plan, and every earlier plan is kept. Chat, icebreakers and photos. Each group gets a live chat to coordinate, Gemini-written icebreakers, and a s

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Mobile app: React Native with Expo SDK 57 and Expo Router, styled with NativeWind, and TanStack Query so the server is always the source of truth. QR codes are scanned with expo-camera and open the app through deep links. API server: Node and TypeScript on Hono, deployed to Netlify Functions. The server makes every AI call and does every database write; the app only reads its own data, protected by row-level security. Data: Supabase Postgres with pgvector for interest similarity, plus Supabase Auth, Realtime (live chat and meetups) and Storage (photos). The first stages of matching run as database functions: walking the connection graph with a recursive SQL query, then ranking by similarity. AI: Google Gemini throughout. gemini-embedding-001 at 768 dimensions for profile embeddings. Gemini Flash, with Flash-Lite as a fallback, to form groups, analyze feedback and write icebreakers. Gemini with Google Maps grounding and the Places API for activity plans, and Ticketmaster Discovery for real events. A shared contract: one TypeScript and Zod package that both the app and the server import. Four of us worked in parallel against mock data, and any mismatch in a request or response broke the build instead of the demo.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Serverless time limits. Netlify ends every request after 10 seconds, and a grounded Gemini call, a Places lookup and a Ticketmaster fallback can take longer than that together. We rebuilt activity planning as a resumable job that runs one step per request. The app drives it to completion, and it picks up where it left off if you close the app. Maps grounding only names the place. It gives a venue's name and Maps link but no coordinates, address or price. We follow each grounded answer with a Places lookup on the place ID it returns. Rate limits and outages. Gemini's free tier regularly gave us quota errors (429) and overload errors (503). Every AI step falls back to something: Flash to Flash-Lite, then a deterministic backup. Matching and planning never fail completely during a demo. Privacy has more ways to leak than you'd expect. We hid unmet people's names and photos on the group screen, then found the AI's explanation still named them ("you and Zoe both know Alex"). Fixing it meant hiding those names from the prompt, rejecting any reply that mentions them, and giving each viewer their own version of the explanation. Making feedback actually matter. Gemini's similarity scores for our profiles all landed between 0.85 and 0.94, so we compare people relative to the rest of the pool instead. Our first feedback boost was also weaker than the shift that re-embedding caused: a "yes, I'd meet again" made a match slightly worse . We raised the boost weight until feedback reliably p

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Feedback measurably changes the next match. In one test on our demo data, one person marking another as someone they'd meet again raised that person's match score from 0.83 to 0.97. devpost_page.tagline: An AI prototype that processes ad creatives, both images and videos, to extract rich visual, textual, and audio insights that reveal brand intent and power next-generation recommendation engines.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The inspiration came from real-world ad recommendation systems like AppLovin’s Axon, which rely on large datasets of ad creatives to predict performance. We wanted to explore how far we could push multimodal intelligence by building a system that understands ad content visually, textually, and acoustically. Our goal was to make ad data more insightful and useful for smarter recommendation models.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: ADLOVIN Media Intelligence processes ad creatives, both images and videos, and extracts high-value multimodal features such as visual composition, text sentiment, and audio mood. These embeddings can then be used to generate creative performance insights or power downstream machine learning models for recommendation and ranking.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built a modular feature extraction pipeline in Python. For video ads, we used FFmpeg to extract keyframes and Librosa for audio signal analysis. Each frame was embedded using a pretrained vision transformer, and text elements were captured through EasyOCR and language models. We used ChromaDB to store and query embeddings at scale, and FastAPI to provide an interface for experimentation and testing.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One major challenge was optimizing feature extraction for large videos while maintaining temporal coherence between visual and audio signals. Another was ensuring meaningful clustering in the vector database without redundant representations, especially after removing the deduplication algorithm. Balancing efficiency and fidelity across multiple modalities required careful design and parameter tuning. One of the major issues faced was the wifi. It made our life really hard. We had to find place to work outside of the venue.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We successfully built an end-to-end multimodal intelligence pipeline that can process a wide range of ad creatives and output interpretable embeddings. The system achieved reliable text and sentiment extraction from frames and robust feature representation using transformer-based models.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to align multimodal embeddings for recommendation tasks, fine-tune vector similarity searches for creative clustering, and manage large-scale ad processing efficiently. We also gained experience combining computer vision, audio analysis, and natural language understanding into one cohesive system.

sections.heading: What's next for ADLOVIN Media Intelligence
sections.text: Next, we plan to add a lightweight deduplication model, connect the embeddings to a performance dataset for supervised learning, and build an interactive dashboard to visualize ad intelligence insights in real time. We also aim to explore generative tools that can use embeddings to suggest creative improvements.

sections.text: During my first ever internship at a startup, I walked in pumped to build new features. Instead, a HUGE chunk of my time went to maintaining the 50+ APIs the company depended on. Users would report that something was broken, and almost every time the cause was the same: an API vendor had shipped a change, and nobody had read the changelog. The truth is, NOBODY reads the changelogs. ever! I don’t blame them. No human can keep up with dozens of vendors shipping changes every single day, constantly rereading changelogs over and over again just in case one of them breaks something. API maintenance is one of the most time-consuming, frustrating pain points in software engineering. I'm not the only one who feels this. Harsha Gaddipati , a fellow Georgia Tech student, former AWS intern and Y Combinator alum, put it perfectly: "Over the past year, I've worked with over 50 API vendors, mostly early-stage startups. One pattern is consistent: API communication is broken. Breaking changes ship with little warning. Useful features quietly launch and go unnoticed. Changelogs don't get read. Heck, when I worked at AWS, over 30% of our service downtime was due to external api/package changes going unnoticed. This friction made sense before agentic coding tools existed. However, now it doesn't." He's completley right. sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Swarm is autonomous API maintenance, like Dependabot but for APIs, except it writes the fix, proves it works, and texts you. SWARM stands for its five stages: Scan: parses your repo (Python AST) and maps every SDK import, API call site and pinned version. Watch: maintains a knowledge base of 4,700+ real changelog entries, SDK releases and OpenAPI specs across popular api vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Stripe, Twilio, GitHub, Plaid, Notion, Resend), refreshed daily by a GitHub Actions job plus a 10-minute poller. 337 breaking changes are catalogued with structured details. Analyze: matches breaking changes against your actual call sites, then an agent confirms whether your code is really affected and how badly. Report: texts you over iMessage through Photon. "Heads up: OpenAI's SDK change broke your repo. Fixing it now." You can steer the fix in plain English, and Swarm asks for your OK before it opens a PR and again before it merges. Mend: Factory's Droid agent writes the fix while every command it runs executes in an isolated Daytona sandbox. Then Swarm independently proves the fix: Droid's regression test must fail on the original code with the real vendor error, and the full test suite must pass on a fresh install of the fixed code. Only then does it offer a PR. On real open-source repos broken by OpenAI's SDK 1.0 change, Swarm goes from connecting the repo to a tested, verified fix in under a minute. Companies take about 48 hours on average to fix a breaking API change, ofte

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Factory Droid SDK (Python) is the Mend agent. It diagnoses the break, edits the code, writes a regression test and revises when Swarm's verification rejects an attempt. Daytona runs every command the agent executes, in a fresh sandbox per fix that cold-starts in about 2 seconds from a prebuilt snapshot. By design, Droid has no shell: its only way to execute code is the sandbox, so agent-written code never touches the host. API keys and the GitHub token never enter the sandbox, and PRs are opened from the host. Photon 2.0 (official Python client) powers the iMessage agent: alerts, two-way steering, standing instructions, and approval-gated PRs and merges, with safe handling of ambiguous replies ("hmm" or "wait" never triggers an action). Claude (Anthropic API) classifies changelogs, writes analysis verdicts and runs the conversational agent. Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite and Server-Sent Events. Frontend: a single HTML file where the live SWARM workflow graph is the interface. Every stage lights up in real time, and clicking any node shows the real evidence behind it.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Making the proof honest. The demo repo's existing tests mocked the removed API, so they passed even on broken code. I rebuilt verification so Swarm runs the agent's new test against the original commit and requires it to fail with the real vendor error. If the test doesn't prove the break, Swarm rejects it and sends the agent back. Sandbox networking. Daytona's network rules blocked the agent's API from inside the sandbox, so I redesigned the architecture so the sandbox is the agent's only way to execute anything. It turned into the strongest security property of the whole system. Speed. Connect-to-fix started at about 2 minutes 15 seconds. Preparing the sandbox the moment a repo connects, giving the agent precise context, and finding why its first attempt kept failing brought it under a minute(a 120% increase in speed!!). Conversational safety. A texting agent that can merge code needs to be careful. Every PR and merge requires a clear yes, and ambiguous replies get a clarifying question instead of an action.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Everything is real end to end: real open-source repos, real vendor breaks, real sandboxes, real PRs and real iMessages. Swarm found a second, hidden bug along the way: one repo silently depended on a package the old OpenAI SDK used to install for it, and the fix declares it properly. A verification guardrail that refuses to trust the agent blindly, which is what makes it safe to merge an AI-written fix from your phone. It survives real failures: page refreshes, server crashes, slow agents and messaging outages all recover cleanly. Once Swarm catches a break, it handles the entire api maintinence worflow about 2,900x faster than the average software company

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: An AI agent is only as trustworthy as the system checking its work. The most valuable part of Swarm isn't only writing the fix, but it's also PROVING the fix works. I also learned how much good engineering lives in the unglamo

devpost_page.tagline: Jesture is a magical gesture-based drawing experience where your hands become the paintbrush! Wave your arms about and watch your beautiful (or hilariously terrible) art manifest on your screen!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The inspiration for Jesture mainly comes from popular fiction. The idea started as one one-off comment by a couple of my friends who thought it would be interesting to be able to control your computer through hand gestures like in Iron Man, where Tony Stark uses hand gestures to control devices or interact with virtual environments. This concept felt futuristic and exciting, but we also saw a practical application: making technology more accessible and intuitive. Gesture-based controls can provide an alternative interface for individuals with limited mobility or those who find traditional input devices like keyboards and mice challenging to use. By combining creativity and accessibility, we aimed to create a tool that is not only fun but also empowers users to interact with technology in a more natural and inclusive way. A paint application is the perfect demo for this new idea as it showcases the potential of gesture-based controls in a highly interactive yet fun way. Drawing is a universal activity that doesn't require any prior technical knowledge, making it accessible to users of all skill levels (even kids, in this case). By allowing users to create art with simple hand movements, the application demonstrates how natural gestures can replace traditional input devices like a mouse or stylus. A paint application also highlights the precision and responsiveness of the gesture recognition system. "The artists" can see immediate feedback as their gestures translate into lines

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Jesture is an interactive drawing and guessing game powered by gesture recognition. Users can draw on a virtual canvas using hand gestures, switch between drawing modes (free draw, line, circle), and have an AI guess what they are drawing. It combines creativity, technology, and fun into one seamless package.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: MediaPipe for real-time hand gesture recognition. Raylib for rendering the drawing canvas and UI. OpenCV for capturing webcam input. Google GenAI for generating AI-based guesses of user drawings. Python as the primary programming language to integrate all these technologies. Tensorflow used to train the hand gesture recognition (thumbs up/thumbs down/pointing/etc.)

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Fine-tuning gesture recognition model to ensure accurate and responsive controls. Managing real-time performance while processing webcam input, rendering graphics, and running AI predictions simultaneously. (Some of my earlier implementations were painfully slow)

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Successfully integrating gesture recognition with a drawing application. Creating an "objectively" fun and interactive experience where AI guesses user drawings. Building a smooth and responsive interface that feels intuitive to use.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: How to work with MediaPipe for gesture recognition and its potential for other applications. The power of Raylib for creating interactive graphics in Python. The importance of optimizing performance when working with real-time systems. How to integrate AI models like Google GenAI into creative projects in a fun way

sections.heading: What's next for Jesture
sections.text: Adding more gesture-based controls? A multiplayer mode update where users can collaborate on drawings? Other platforms like mobile?

devpost_page.title: Market Melee
devpost_page.tagline: Have you ever wanted to trade stocks, but don't have the money to do so? Perhaps, maybe you want to battle it out against fellow traders? Market Melee is the perfect stock sandbox for you!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Our inspiration for Market Melee stemmed from the entire group taking an Introduction to Computational Investing class. After seeing how a lot of financial jargon, calculations, and visualizations are intimidating to the everyday person, we decided to build Market Melee to make stock market investing more accessible and engaging for everyone. By gamifying the investing experience, we aimed to create a platform where any user can learn, compete, and grow their financial knowledge in a fun environment.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Market Melee is a web application that allows users to create and manage simulated stock portfolios using real-time market data. Having hundreds of stocks to choose from, notably from the S&P 500, they are able to allocate their investments and track their portfolio performance over time. Features include interactive graphs, detailed stock metrics, and a place to track your own progress against friends within your league.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Market Melee using Python and the Flask web framework for our backend, and utilized MongoDB Atlas as our database to store user information, and stock statistics. For our data analysis and visualization, we used libraries such as pandas, NumPy, and MatPlotLib to read stock information and generate performance graphs. The frontend was developed with HTML, CSS, with Bootstrap for responsive design, Javascript to add interactive features, and Jinja to wrap it all nicely with our Flask backend.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of the main challenges we ran into was displaying our data visualization graphs onto our frontend, as we had to decide whether we were to store our images via cloud, storage, or make them temporary images. Furthermore, git version control was another massive hurdle we had to face, as oftentimes the backend and the frontend had conflicting files, which lead to multiple merge conflicts. Authentication and managing users was also a tough task, as we had to make sure users are only able to see their information, while also storing and utilizing other users' data at the same time.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of creating a platform that helps bridge the gap between stock investors and the everyday person. Furthermore, we are very happy about how our main features of individualized stock statistics and visualizations worked seamlessly with our frontend, which allows users to view individual stocks and learn more about them, using pop-up modals to learn more about stock statistics, such as daily returns, volatility, and even the Sharpe Ratio.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: While developing Market Melee, we improved our ability to work with a foreign stack for web development, as navigating through this was slow at first. Furthermore, we learned how to effectively leverage document-oriented databases like MongoDB and Flask for routing and session management. Furthermore, we strengthened our ability to delegate tasks in order to have a smooth work flow and proper code management.

sections.heading: What's next for Market Melee
sections.text: Looking in the future, we plan on incorporate more league functionality such as live-server drafting between users to mimic for users who want to mimic actual drafting of limited stock options. We also hope to implement machine learning and more advanced algorithms to help users leverage technology to their advantage to profit from the stock market. In addition, we would want to implement more educational resources within the platforms to help users grow financial literacy and their own portfolios.
